claim: The expression limit of GFP was about 15% of the total cellular protein in S. cerevisiae.
source: We estimated that the expression limit of a green fluorescent protein (GFP) was about 15% of the total cellular protein in S. cerevisiae (Kintaka et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kintaka et al., 2016).

claim: GFP is a highly structured cytoplasmic protein unrelated to the cellular functions of yeast and thus harmless.
source: Because GFP is a highly structured cytoplasmic protein unrelated to the cellular functions of yeast and thus harmless, this level could be considered the expression limit for any protein that causes growth defects triggered by the protein-burden effect.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about GFP's properties and its lack of interaction with yeast cellular functions.

claim: The expression limits of some glycolytic proteins were up to 15% of the total cellular protein.
source: The limits of some glycolytic proteins were up to 15% of the total cellular protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically protein expression measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: The expression limits of glycolytic proteins were independent of the proteins' catalytic activities.
source: These limits were independent of the proteins' catalytic activities, a finding that was supported by an in silico analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from catalytic center mutants (Figure 3) and computational modeling (Figure 4).

claim: Some proteins had low expression limits that were explained by their localization and metabolic perturbations.
source: Some proteins had low expression limits that were explained by their localization and metabolic perturbations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that removal of mitochondrial targeting sequence from Adh3 increased its expression limit (Figure 3C-D) and metabolic measurements (Figure 5).

claim: The codon usage should be highly optimized to trigger the protein-burden effect, even under strong transcriptional induction.
source: The codon usage should be highly optimized to trigger the protein-burden effect, even under strong transcriptional induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that proteins with low codon optimality (Glk1, Pyk2, Pdc6) had lower expression levels, and codon optimization of GLK1 increased its expression (Figure 6).

claim: The S–S-bond-connected aggregation mediated by the cysteine residues of a protein might affect its expression limit.
source: The S–S-bond-connected aggregation mediated by the cysteine residues of a protein might affect its expression limit.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that cysteine-less mutants of Tpi1 had higher expression limits (Figure 8) and that aggregates disappeared after DTT treatment (Figure 7B).

claim: Only non-harmful proteins could be expressed up to the protein-burden limit.
source: Theoretically, only non-harmful proteins could be expressed up to the protein-burden limit.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the protein burden concept.

claim: All cells expressing glycolytic proteins, with the exceptions of those expressing HXT1, HXT3, and HXT4, showed significant growth retardation compared to the vector control cells in low-copy conditions.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, all cells expressing glycolytic proteins, with the exceptions of those expressing HXT1, HXT3, and HXT4, showed significant growth retardation compared to the vector control cells in low-copy conditions (p<0.01, Welch's t-test, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate measurements shown in Figure 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: The copy numbers of all gTOW plasmids containing target genes were significantly lower than those containing the empty vector.
source: The copy numbers of all gTOW plasmids containing target genes were significantly lower than those containing the empty vector (p<0.05, Welch's t-test, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental plasmid copy number measurements shown in Figure 1D-E with statistical analysis.

claim: Most glycolytic proteins were expressed at levels high enough to make them visible within the SDS-PAGE–separated whole cellular proteins.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, most proteins were expressed at levels high enough to make them visible within the SDS-PAGE–separated whole cellular proteins
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental protein expression data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression levels of Pgk1, Gmp1, Eno2, and Eno1 were higher than that of GFP.
source: the expression levels of Pgk1, Gmp1, Eno2, and Eno1 were higher than that of GFP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental protein expression measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The expression levels of Pfk1, Adh3, and Hxts were almost undetectable with this experimental system.
source: By contrast, the expression levels of Pfk1, Adh3, and Hxts were almost undetectable with this experimental system.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental protein expression measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The expression of some proteins was increased more than 10,000-fold in this experimental system.
source: The expression of some proteins was increased more than 10,000-fold in this experimental system.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Overexpression of Pfk1, Adh3, and Hxts seemed harmful because their copy numbers were lower than those of the other proteins.
source: Overexpression of Pfk1, Adh3, and Hxts seemed harmful because their copy numbers were lower than the those of the other proteins (red circles in Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the relationship between copy number and protein expression shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The expression of Glk1, Pyk2, and Pdc6 seemed to be repressed because their copy numbers were higher than those of the other proteins.
source: By contrast, the expression of Glk1, Pyk2, and Pdc6 seemed to be repressed because their copy numbers were higher than those of the other proteins (blue circles in Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the relationship between copy number and protein expression shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the expression levels and plasmid copy numbers.
source: there was no significant correlation between the expression levels and plasmid copy numbers (Pearson r=0.28, p=0.12).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The expression levels of all proteins except Pfk1, Fba1, Tdh3, and Eno1 were not significantly changed by introducing mutations into catalytic centers.
source: The expression levels of all proteins except Pfk1, Fba1, Tdh3, and Eno1 were not significantly changed by introducing mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing wild-type and catalytic center mutant expression levels shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The expression levels of mutant Pfk1 and Tdh3 were significantly higher than those of wild-type proteins.
source: The expression levels of mutant Pfk1 and Tdh3 were significantly higher than those of wild-type proteins
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis (p<0.05, Welch's t-test).

claim: The expression levels of mutant Fba1 and Pgk1 were significantly lower than those of wild-type proteins.
source: the expression levels of mutant Fba1 and Pgk1were significantly lower than those of wild-type proteins (p<0.05, Welch's t-test, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: The expression level of mutant Pfk2 significantly increased when compared with that of wild-type Pfk2.
source: The expression level of mutant Pfk2 significantly increased when compared with that of wild-type Pfk2 (p=0.046, Welch's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: The expression limits of most of the glycolytic proteins studied are not restricted by metabolic perturbations triggered by their overproduction.
source: We concluded that the expression limits of most of the glycolytic proteins studied here are not restricted by metabolic perturbations triggered by their overproduction
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from catalytic center mutants (Figure 3A) and computational modeling (Figure 4).

claim: The expression limits of Pfk1 and Pfk2 are exceptionally restricted by metabolic perturbations.
source: whereas the expression limits of Pfk1 and Pfk2 are exceptionally restricted by metabolic perturbations.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing that catalytic center mutants of Pfk1 and Pfk2 had higher expression limits (Figure 3A-B).

claim: The expression level of ΔMTS-Adh3 was about three times higher than that of wild-type Adh3.
source: As shown in Figure 3C and D, the expression level of ΔMTS-Adh3 was about three times higher than that of wild-type Adh3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The mitochondrial localization of Adh3 restricts its expression limit.
source: We concluded that the mitochondrial localization of Adh3 restricts its expression limit, probably because the high-level expression of this mitochondrial protein causes growth defects due to overloading of mitochondrial transport resources (Kintaka et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that removal of the mitochondrial targeting sequence increased Adh3 expression (Figure 3C-D) and a citation to previous work.

claim: Overproduction of 14 of 20 glycolytic proteins did not cause more than a two-fold metabolic change in simulations.
source: Overproduction of 14 of 20 glycolytic proteins did not cause more than a two-fold metabolic change (gray lines in Figure 4A)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpression of most glycolytic proteins does not cause serious metabolic perturbations.
source: indicating that overexpression of most glycolytic proteins does not cause serious metabolic perturbations.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The overproduction of Hxk1 and Hxk2 affected glycolytic metabolism throughout in simulations.
source: By contrast, the overproduction of Hxk1 and Hxk2 affected glycolytic metabolism throughout
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The overproduction of Pdc1 and Cdc19 affected metabolism locally in simulations.
source: and the overproduction of Pdc1 and Cdc19 affected metabolism locally (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Simultaneous overproduction of both Pfk1 and Pfk2 caused severe metabolic changes in simulations.
source: Simultaneous overproduction of both Pfk1 and Pfk2 caused severe metabolic changes (Figure 4D)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Overexpression of both wild-type and CC mutant Pfk2 triggered significant reductions in some metabolites.
source: Overexpression of both wild-type and CC mutant Pfk2 triggered significant reductions in some metabolites (p<0.05, Welch's t-test, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5A with statistical analysis.

claim: The level of F16bP in the cells overexpressing wild-type Pfk2 was >3-fold higher than that in the CC mutant Pfk2.
source: We noticed, however, that the level of F16bP in the cells overexpressing wild-type Pfk2 was >3-fold higher than that in the CC mutant Pfk2 (Figure 5A, p<0.05, Welch's t-test, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5A with statistical analysis.

claim: Levels of glycolytic metabolites in the cells overexpressing wild-type Pfk1 and Tdh3 were not changed more than three-fold over the vector control.
source: As shown in Figure 5B and C, levels of glycolytic metabolites in the cells overexpressing wild-type Pfk1 and Tdh3 were not changed more than three-fold over the vector control.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Overexpression of Pfk1 and Tdh3 did not trigger significant metabolic changes through their catalytic activities.
source: We thus concluded that overexpression of Pfk1 and Tdh3 did not trigger significant metabolic changes through their catalytic activities, at least in the detected glycolytic metabolites.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The expression levels of Glk1 and Pyk2 were significantly elevated in high-copy conditions.
source: Moreover, the expression levels of Glk1 and Pyk2 were significantly elevated in high-copy conditions (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental protein expression measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GLK1, PYK2, and PDC6 had a much lower tAIg than the other glycolytic genes.
source: we analyzed the tRNA adaptation index of a gene (tAIg) (Tuller et al., 2010) for the the glycolytic genes studied here (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and noticed that GLK1, PYK2, and PDC6 had a much lower tAIg than the other glycolytic genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of codon usage shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Glk1 expressed from CoGLK1 was present at levels 3.6 and 4.7 times higher than that expressed from native GLK1 in low- and high-copy conditions, respectively.
source: Glk1 expressed from CoGLK1 was present at levels 3.6 and 4.7 times higher than that expressed from native GLK1 in low- and high-copy conditions, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental protein expression measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Glk1 expression was low due to its low codon optimality.
source: We concluded that Glk1 expression was low due to its low codon optimality.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing that codon optimization increased Glk1 expression (Figure 6A).

claim: The codon usage of GLK1 was not optimized to maximize their translation after the diauxic shift.
source: Because the lag times were not significantly different (p=0.44), we concluded that the codon usage of GLK1 was not optimized to maximize their translation after the diauxic shift.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental measurements of GFP expression timing shown in Figure 6C-D with statistical analysis.

claim: Cysteines were responsible for creating the high-molecular-weight bands in Pgk1 and Eno2 experiments.
source: We confirmed that cysteines were responsible for creating these bands because they disappeared when cysteine residues were removed from Pgk1 and Eno2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that cysteine-less mutants did not form the bands (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Glycolytic proteins, translational elongation factors, and translation initiation factors were mainly detected in the high-molecular-weight bands.
source: As shown in Figure 7C and D, we mainly detected glycolytic proteins, translational elongation factors, and translation initiation factors, in addition to each overexpressed protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS analysis data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: The aggregation did not seem to affect the expression limits of Eno3 and Pgk1.
source: This aggregation did not seem to affect the expression limits of Eno3 and Pgk1 because the expression limits of wild-type proteins and cysteine-less mutants (Eno2-C248S and Pgk1-C98S) were indistinguishable (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data comparing expression limits of wild-type and cysteine-less mutants shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tpi1 constituted many aggregation bands upon its overexpression.
source: As shown in Figure 8A, Tpi1 constituted many aggregation bands upon its overexpression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The majority of Tpi1 aggregation bands disappeared when cysteine residues were removed from Tpi1 or after DTT treatment.
source: The majority of these bands disappeared when cysteine residues were removed from Tpi1 (C41S, C126S), or after DTT treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The expression levels of cysteine-less Tpi1 significantly increased above those of wild-type Tpi1.
source: As shown in Figure 8B, the expression levels of cysteine-less Tpi1 significantly increased above those of wild-type Tpi1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B with statistical analysis.

claim: The removal of cysteine residues would not only prevent the formation of aggregates but would also increase the expression limit of Tpi1.
source: Because mutant Tpi1 levels were higher than wild-type Tpi1 levels, even in +DTT conditions, the removal of cysteine residues would not only prevent the formation of aggregates but would also increase the expression limit of Tpi1.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The protein-burden limit of S. cerevisiae cells is around 15% of the total cellular protein.
source: In conclusion, we established the ultimate expression level that causes cellular growth defects due to the protein-burden effect as around 15% of the total cellular protein.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from GFP expression (cited from Kintaka et al., 2016) and glycolytic protein expression measurements in this study.

claim: Pgk1 and Eno2 are 1.5-fold larger than Gpm1.
source: Although Pgk1 (44.7 kDa) and Eno2 (46.9 kDa) are 1.5-fold larger than Gpm1 (27.6 kDa), their expression limits were similar to those of Gpm1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of protein molecular weights and experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A protein's size does not affect its expression limit, at least for proteins in the molecular weight range of glycolytic proteins.
source: These results suggest that a protein's size does not affect its expression limit, at least for proteins in this molecular weight range.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing expression limits of proteins with different sizes.

claim: The expression limits of proteins are not determined by the molar concentrations of those proteins but by the cost of the protein production.
source: These data also suggest that the expression limits of proteins are not determined by the molar concentrations of those proteins but by the cost of the protein production.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that proteins of different sizes had similar expression limits when measured in AU.

claim: Pfk1 and Pfk2 form a hetero-octameric complex.
source: Pfk1 and Pfk2 form a hetero-octameric complex, and their stoichiometric imbalance leads to the formation of filamentous Pfk1 structures in the cytosol (Schwock et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Schwock et al., 2004).

claim: Stoichiometric imbalance of Pfk1 and Pfk2 leads to the formation of filamentous Pfk1 structures in the cytosol.
source: Pfk1 and Pfk2 form a hetero-octameric complex, and their stoichiometric imbalance leads to the formation of filamentous Pfk1 structures in the cytosol (Schwock et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Schwock et al., 2004).

claim: Fba1 is an essential homodimeric enzyme.
source: For example, Fba1 is an essential homodimeric enzyme (UniProtKB: P14540).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the UniProtKB database.

claim: The catalytic activity of Tdh3 (C150G mutation) affects transcriptional silencing through interaction with Sir2 protein.
source: Beside its metabolic function, Tdh3 directly binds to Sir2 protein to promote transcriptional silencing, and a mutation in the catalytic center (C150G) reduces the silencing (Ringel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Ringel et al., 2013).

claim: The overexpression of 14 bidirectional enzymes showed minor metabolic changes in simulations.
source: To support this idea, the overexpression of 14 bidirectional enzymes showed minor metabolic changes, whereas the overexpression of 6 unidirectional enzymes (including Hxks, Pfks, Cdc19, and Pdc1) showed strong metabolic changes in the simulation (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The overexpression of 6 unidirectional enzymes (including Hxks, Pfks, Cdc19, and Pdc1) showed strong metabolic changes in simulations.
source: To support this idea, the overexpression of 14 bidirectional enzymes showed minor metabolic changes, whereas the overexpression of 6 unidirectional enzymes (including Hxks, Pfks, Cdc19, and Pdc1) showed strong metabolic changes in the simulation (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The codon optimality of Glk1 (tAIg = 0.38) is close to the average for all the yeast genes (tAIg = 0.37).
source: Actually, the codon optimality of Glk1 (tAIg = 0.38) is close to the average for all the yeast genes (tAIg = 0.37)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of codon usage.

claim: The codon optimality of most yeast genes is not high enough to allow expression of their proteins up to the protein-burden limit, even if they are expressed from a strong promoter on a multicopy plasmid.
source: These observations suggest that the codon optimality of most yeast genes is not high enough to allow expression of their proteins up to the protein-burden limit, even if they are expressed from a strong promoter on a multicopy plasmid.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from codon optimality analysis and experimental expression data.

claim: S–S-bond-mediated protein aggregation occurs even in normal physiological conditions.
source: Therefore, we speculated that the S–S-bond-mediated protein aggregation occurs even in normal physiological conditions, but it is accelerated by an increase in the concentration of cytoplasmic proteins upon overexpression of glycolytic proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from LC-MS/MS data showing the same proteins detected in vector control samples at lower levels.

claim: The most highly expressed glycolytic protein Gpm1 does not have a cysteine residue.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the fact that the most highly expressed glycolytic protein Gpm1, which has a molecular weight similar to that of Tpi1, does not have a cysteine residue.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of protein sequences.

claim: Cdc19 aggregates in a stress-induced and reversible manner through a region of low compositional complexity.
source: Cdc19, one of the glycolytic proteins studied here, aggregates in a stress-induced and reversible manner through a region of low compositional complexity (Saad et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Saad et al., 2017).

claim: Glycolytic proteins are less structurally disordered.
source: We do not think that this mechanism caused growth defects upon overexpression of the glycolytic proteins studied here because they are less structurally disordered (Moriya, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Moriya, 2015).

claim: Glycolytic proteins are not nucleic-acid-binding proteins.
source: and not nucleic-acid-binding proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about glycolytic protein functions.

claim: Protein overexpression is sometimes harmful to cellular growth.
source: Protein overexpression is sometimes harmful to cellular growth (Makanae et al., 2013; Sopko et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Resource overload is triggered upon overexpression of a protein that has a high demand of cellular resources.
source: Resource overload, stoichiometric imbalance, promiscuous interaction, and pathway modulation are triggered upon overexpression of, respectively, (i) a protein that has a high demand of cellular resources (Dong et al., 1995; Kintaka et al., 2016; Stoebel et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Stoichiometric imbalance is triggered upon overexpression of a protein that is part of a protein complex.
source: (ii) a protein that is part of a protein complex (Kaizu et al., 2010; Makanae et al., 2013; Papp et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Promiscuous interaction is triggered upon overexpression of a protein with a nonspecific interaction domain.
source: (iii) a protein with a nonspecific interaction domain (Ma et al., 2010; Vavouri et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pathway modulation is triggered upon overexpression of a protein that catalyzes a pathway.
source: (iv) a protein that catalyzes a pathway (Prelich, 2012; Youn et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The ultimate overexpression of a protein could be harmful for cellular growth because it monopolizes and depletes limited resources involved in protein production.
source: The ultimate overexpression of a protein could be harmful for cellular growth, because it monopolizes and depletes limited resources that are involved in protein production, such as ribosomes and aminoacyl-tRNAs (Gong et al., 2006; Shachrai et al., 2010; Vind et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The protein burden/cost effect is a phenomenon where ultimate protein overexpression is harmful due to resource depletion.
source: This phenomenon is known as the protein burden/cost effect (Kafri et al., 2016; Snoep et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work defining the protein burden concept.

claim: The gTOW method can be used to estimate the expression limit of a target protein that triggers growth defects in S. cerevisiae.
source: We previously developed a genetic tug-of-war (gTOW) method that can be used to estimate the expression limit of a target protein that triggers growth defects in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Makanae et al., 2013; Moriya et al., 2006 , 2012 ).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work describing the gTOW method.

claim: The copy number of the gTOW plasmid inside the cell inversely reflects the deleterious effect of protein expression from the plasmid.
source: As previously reported, the copy number of the gTOW plasmid inside the cell inversely reflects the deleterious effect of protein expression from the plasmid due to the gTOW effect: the plasmid copy number is low if expression of the target protein is harmful to cellular growth, and high if expression of the target protein is less harmful (Kintaka et al., 2016; Makanae et al., 2013; Moriya et al., 2006, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work describing the gTOW mechanism.

claim: Adh3 is a mitochondrial protein.
source: Among the glycolytic proteins tested in this study, Adh3 alone is a mitochondrial protein (Young and Pilgrim, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Glk1 expression increases after a diauxic shift.
source: Glk1 expression increases after a diauxic shift—a growth-phase shift triggered by the carbon source alteration from glucose to ethanol (Zampar et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Codon optimality strongly contributes to translational elongation rate and mRNA stability.
source: Codon optimality strongly contributes totranslational elongation rate and mRNA stability (Presnyak et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Highly expressed proteins are evolved to avoid low translational robustness, low folding stability, or a high propensity for misinteraction.
source: In general, highly expressed proteins such as glycolytic proteins are thus evolved to avoid these characteristics (Zhang and Yang, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Concentration-dependent liquid phase separation is considered to cause toxicity upon overexpression of structurally disordered and nucleic-acid-binding proteins.
source: Concentration-dependent liquid phase separation is also considered to cause toxicity upon overexpression of structurally disordered and nucleic-acid-binding proteins (Bolognesi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PFK1 and PFK2 were expressed from the PYK1/CDC19 promoter because their expression from the TDH3 promoter was too strong and the growth of the transformants was very poor.
source: PFK1 and PFK2 were exceptionally expressed from the less-strong PYK1/CDC19 promoter because their expression from the TDH3 promoter was too strong and consequently the growth of the transformants was very poor (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations (though data not shown).

claim: The maximum growth rates of cells with the vector in +leucine conditions are much greater than those in –leucine conditions.
source: In this experimental system, the maximum growth rates of the cells with the vector in +leucine conditions are much greater than those in –leucine conditions (see Figure 1B–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth rate data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The copy number of leu2-89 is not sufficient to support fully the leucine requirement in –leucine conditions.
source: probably because the copy number of leu2-89 is not sufficient tosupport fully the leucine requirement in –leucine conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the growth rate difference between conditions.

claim: The expression levels produced under low-copy conditions were already sufficient to cause growth defects for most of the 29 target proteins.
source: We measured the expression limits of most of the 29 target proteins in low-copy conditions because the expression levels produced under these conditions were already sufficient to cause growth defects.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations of growth defects shown in Figure 1.

claim: The relationship between AU and percentage of total protein is % total protein = 5.5 × AU.
source: The relationship between the AU and the percentage of total protein that we previously reported (Kintaka et al., 2016) was estimated, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, as % total protein = 5.5 × AU.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental calibration data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The metabolic flux should be determined only by the availability of substrates when the concentrations of bidirectional enzymes are more than a certain level.
source: The reason why their overexpression does not cause metabolic perturbations is probably that they are bidirectional enzymes: the metabolic flux should be determined only by the availability of substrates when the concentrations of these enzymes are more than a certain level.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on enzyme kinetics principles.

claim: The expression limits of ΔMTS-Adh3 and CoGlk1 are still lower than those of other high limit proteins such as Pgk1 and Gpm1.
source: The expression limits of ΔMTS-Adh3 (0.45 AU, Figure 3D) and CoGlkl (1.07 AU, Figure 6A) are still lower than those of other high limit proteins such as Pgk1 and Gpm1 (2.26 AU and 2.63 AU, respectively, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental protein expression data from multiple figures.

claim: Multiple mechanisms restrict the expression limits of Adh3 and Glk1.
source: It is thus likely that multiple mechanisms restrict the expression limits of these proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that removing single factors did not bring expression limits to the maximum level.
